slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter twenty-seven: the examination of views.

slides.heading: Was I someone before this life?
points: Will I be someone after it?
Has the world always existed? Will it end?
The Buddha refused to answer. Why was he right?
slides.say: Was I someone before this life? Will I be someone after it? Has the world always existed, and will it ever end? These are some of the oldest questions people ask, and some of the most anxious. In the Buddha's time teachers built whole systems on their answers, and the Buddha famously refused to answer them at all. This last chapter asks why the refusal was right.

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: One tool: the same as what it depends on, or different?
Applied to the self of past and future lives
Then to the world; and the text ends with a bow
slides.say: It gathers up the whole work. The tool is one used again and again since chapter one: is the thing the same as what it depends on, or different from it? Applied to the self of past and future lives, both answers fail, as they failed for fire and fuel in chapter ten and for the self in chapter eighteen. Then the views about the world fail in the same way. The text ends where it began: with a bow to the Buddha, who taught in order to let go of all views.

slides.heading: The verses
points: The last thirty verses, newly translated
The Sanskrit is shown above each verse
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Views that rest on a beginning and an end
slides.say: Now the explanation. The chapter opens with a list. One group of views looks back: I existed in the past, I did not exist, and with them the world is permanent, the world is not permanent. These rest on the earlier limit, a beginning. The other group looks forward: I will exist, I will not exist, I will be someone else, and the world has an end, it has no end. These rest on the later limit. Each question has the familiar four corners: yes, no, both, neither. The views differ in content, but each takes for granted a self or a world with a nature of its own, which could have a beginning or an end.

slides.heading: Did I exist in the past?
slides.say: Take the first view: I existed in the past. Suppose you are that very person from an earlier life. But a person is made of a body, feelings, perceptions, habits and awareness, what the verses call what is taken up. The body of that earlier person is gone; the feelings and thoughts are gone. So what stayed the same? Not something apart from body and mind: such a self is never found. Not the aggregates themselves: they pass away moment by moment, and what is taken up cannot be the one who takes it up, any more than the fuel is the fire. Not other than them: then it would be seen on its own, and it never is. But not nothing either. Verse twenty-seven point eight says so plainly: the self is not non-existent either, and that is the conclusion. Like the chariot, the self is designated in dependence on its parts: not found when sought, and still able to act.

slides.heading: Or did I not exist?
slides.say: Then perhaps the opposite: the person in the earlier life was someone entirely other than you. This fails in the other direction. If you were wholly other than that earlier person, you could exist even if that person had never lived. The connection that makes it a series of lives would be gone. And the consequences matter. The stream would be cut off. What was done would be lost, or one person would act and a stranger would reap the result. Nor could you simply come into being from nothing, with no past at all, for that would be arising without a cause, which chapter one ruled out. So none of the four views about the past holds, and the views about the future fall in exactly the same way. What links the lives is not a traveller passing over, and not a gap. It is continuity designated on a series that is neither the same nor different, like one flame lit from another. This is the middle way between the two great fears: that something of me must last for ever, and that at death I am simply wiped out.

slides.heading: God and human: permanent or not?
points: Exactly the same: permanent, and never born
Wholly other: no continuity at all
Permanent and impermanent are named together
slides.say: Verses fifteen to twenty test the views about permanence with a traditional example: a being reborn as a god and later as a human. If the god and the human were exactly the same, the being would be permanent; but then it would never have been born, for what is permanent is not born. If the human were wholly other than the god, there would be no continuity between them at all. Half god and half human will not do either, and if both cannot be established, neither can neither. Verse nineteen adds a quiet point: if someone came from somewhere and went on elsewhere, samsara would be one traveller walking for ever. But there is no such someone. And if nothing is found that is permanent, nothing is found to be impermanent either. Like long and short, they are named together.

slides.heading: Does the world have an end?
slides.say: The last group of views looks to the future of the world. If the world had an end, how could there be a next world? If it were endless, how could there be a next one either? Both pictures freeze the world: one cuts it off, the other makes it one unending thing. The answer is the lamp. The continuum of the aggregates goes on like the flame of a lamp. The flame at midnight is not the flame at dusk; the oil and air that feed it have all been replaced. Yet it is not an unrelated flame; each moment of burning arises in dependence on the one before. Such a series is neither endless nor with an end, because there is no single thing there to last for ever or to stop. Could part of the world end and part go on? Then part of the person would perish and part would not, and a person is not split into a lasting half and a perishing half.

slides.heading: All views let go
points: Since all things are empty, where would views arise?
Abandoned: views that grasp at own-nature
Right view is not one more thing to cling to
slides.say: Then the chapter steps back. Since all things are empty, says Nagarjuna, where would views like permanent arise, for whom, which ones, and why? In the end the sixteen views do not need to be refuted one by one. They lose their footing all at once, because each needed a self or a world with a nature of its own to be about. Letting go of all views does not mean having no opinions, or refusing to say anything. Nagarjuna has argued all through the book, and the Buddha taught for decades. Chandrakirti and Tsongkhapa read it this way: what is abandoned are views that grasp at things as existing from their own side. Right view, the seeing of emptiness, is not one more thing to cling to; it is what loosens the clinging.

slides.heading: A bow to Gautama
points: He taught, out of compassion, to let go of all views
The first chapter opened with the same bow
'Taking up' compassion: the word for designation
slides.say: And the text ends as it began, with a bow, in verse twenty-seven point thirty: to Gautama, who out of compassion taught the true Dharma so that all views could be let go. The first chapter opened with a bow to the Buddha who taught dependent arising as the quieting of elaborations. The last closes with a bow to the same teacher for the same gift. Even here the key word of the work returns: he taught taking up compassion, the word used for designation in dependence. The teaching, too, arose in dependence: on compassion, for those who suffer.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: Past and future lives, and the weight of what we do
The mere I keeps its promises and meets its results
Removed: the traveller, and the one wiped out at death
slides.say: None of this denies past lives, future lives, or the moral weight of what we do. Continuity is kept: one life conditions the next, as one flame lights another, and actions bear their results. Responsibility is kept: the mere I designated on body and mind keeps its promises and meets the results of what it has done. What is removed is the traveller, the self that would walk unchanged from life to life, and its shadow, the self that would be wiped out at death. The fear of both goes with them.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: An old photograph of yourself as a child
Not simply the same; not simply someone else
You, as designated, with nothing travelling the years
slides.say: Try it with an old photograph of yourself as a child. Is that child you? Not simply: every cell, every thought has changed. Someone else? Not simply: your family, your memories and your name run straight from that afternoon to this one. Neither the same nor different, the child is you as designated. Nothing had to travel through the years for that to be true.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: Chapters 8 and 9
Death and Continuity (bonus article)
Talks: Carrierless Continuity; Core Logic 2
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World, chapter nine, on continuity without persistence, where the same person is designated on moments that are neither identical nor wholly different, with the candle burning through the night; and chapter eight, on Nagasena's lamp, neither the same nor another. The bonus article Death and Continuity takes up the candle and Tsongkhapa's mere I. Two talks on YouTube take it up too: Carrierless Continuity, and Core Logic Two, on the same logic of identity and difference. Links to all of them are on the chapter page.

slides.heading: The whole text in one bow
points: Each chapter: is it found standing on its own?
Same as what it depends on, or other? Both fail
And it is still there, working, as designated
slides.say: Looking back over the twenty-seven chapters, one movement repeats. Each chapter takes something we are sure of, conditions, motion, the senses, the self, time, the Buddha, nirvana, and asks whether it is found standing on its own. Each time it asks whether the thing is the same as what it depends on or other than it, and each time both answers fail. And each time, the thing is still there, working, as designated: the sprout grows, the walker walks, the fire burns, the path leads to freedom. That is what the homage of chapter one promised: dependent arising, without arising and without ceasing, without coming and without going, the quieting of elaborations, peace. The text does not end in a new theory. It ends in letting go, and in gratitude.
